w: Complete by about 1400, Exeter Cathedral holds the longest uninterrupted medieval stone vaulted ceiling in the world, running the length of its nave in an unbroken ribbed sweep. It also keeps an early set of misericords and a working astronomical clock, seat of the Bishop of Exeter since the Middle Ages.
s: The world's longest unbroken medieval stone vault
_facts: Complete by about 1400
Longest uninterrupted medieval stone vaulted ceiling in the world
Has an early set of misericords
Houses a working astronomical clock

w: Built into Exeter's Roman walls from 1068 after the city's rebellion against William the Conqueror, besieged three months by King Stephen in 1136. The Devon witches, England's last people executed for witchcraft, were tried here in 1682. Its Norman gatehouse survives amid Rougemont Gardens.
s: Where England's last witchcraft trial was held
_facts: Built from 1068 into the Roman city walls, after Exeter's revolt
Besieged for three months by King Stephen in 1136
Devon Witches tried and convicted here in 1682, England's last witchcraft executions
Norman gatehouse survives; site now surrounded by Rougemont Gardens

w: Begun in 1190 and finished by 1214, this is the oldest surviving large medieval bridge in Britain, and the only one still carrying a chapel. At up to 590 feet long with 17 or 18 arches, it once carried shops and houses across the Exe's marshy floodplain, funded by merchants Nicholas and Walter Gervase.
s: Britain's oldest bridge, once lined with shops
_facts: Built 1190-1214; oldest surviving large medieval bridge in Britain
Only British medieval bridge still carrying a chapel
About 590 feet long with 17-18 arches
Funded by merchants Nicholas and Walter Gervase; once carried shops and houses

w: Often called the first building in England to be called a hotel, opened in Cathedral Yard and trading for two centuries. Gutted by fire in October 2016, its restoration crawled through ownership changes and stalled plans; work finally began in January 2026, completion expected 2027.
s: England's first hotel, still rebuilding after fire
_facts: Often described as the first building in England called a hotel
Severely damaged by fire in October 2016
Sold multiple times since; restoration plans repeatedly stalled
Construction restarted 28 January 2026, expected complete 2027

w: A granite War Cross by Sir Edwin Lutyens, hewn from a single block quarried at Haytor on Dartmoor and unveiled by the Prince of Wales in 1921. It stands on Cathedral Green in line with the altar, one of only two Lutyens war crosses doubling as a civic memorial, after a plan for a memorial cloister ran out of money.
s: A Lutyens cross carved from a single Dartmoor block
_facts: Designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens, one of fifteen similar War Crosses
Carved from a single granite block quarried at Haytor, Dartmoor
Unveiled by the Prince of Wales, 16 May 1921
One of only two Lutyens crosses serving as a civic memorial

w: A small Norman-featured church of red sandstone where Exeter's mayor and merchants worshipped through the 14th to 16th centuries. Its Arches name likely comes from a vanished medieval arched thoroughfare that once ran alongside it. Grade I listed.
_facts: Retains many Norman features
Worship place for the Mayor of Exeter and merchants, 14th-16th centuries
Built largely of red sandstone
Grade I listed

w: Built in 1760, the year of George III's coronation, as a Presbyterian meeting house. Sold in 1987, it briefly became an antiques centre before JD Wetherspoon reopened it as a pub in 2005, preserving the original chapel features intact behind the beer taps. Grade I listed.
s: A Presbyterian chapel now pouring pints as a pub
_facts: Built 1760, coronation year of George III
Originally a Presbyterian chapel and meeting house
Sold 1987; became a JD Wetherspoon pub in 2005
Grade I listed; original features preserved

n: Royal Albert Memorial Museum & Art Gallery
w: Exeter's largest museum, founded in 1868 and housed in a Gothic Revival building of local New Red Sandstone. RAMM holds over a million objects spanning zoology, anthropology, fine art and archaeology, a fraction on display. A four-year, 24 million pound redevelopment saw it reopen in December 2011 to a run of awards.
